interest: Chinese press called Inukai's 1932 assassination a fascist coup; reports trace the Kokumin Dōmei, Japan's first fascist party.
overview: This file (894.00F, File 767) comprises U.S. State Department records from April to December 1932 documenting the rise of fascism, reactionary societies, and right-wing extremism in Japan. The file contains cross-reference sheets and diplomatic reporting from the U.S. Embassy in Tokyo (under Chargé d'Affaires Edwin L. Neville), the U.S. Legation in Peiping (under Minister Nelson T. Johnson), and the State Department's Division of Far Eastern Affairs. Major subjects include the ideological definition of Japanese 'Fascio' and its relationship to traditional reactionary patriotic organizations and proletarian parties; the May 15, 1932 assassination of Prime Minister Inukai Tsuyoshi by radical naval and army officers; an exhaustive multi-page compilation of Chinese editorial opinion analyzing the assassination as a fascist coup that doomed Japanese parliamentary democracy and portended heightened military aggression in China; and the formation in late 1932 of the Kokumin Domei (National League) as Japan's first overtly fascist parliamentary party.

subfiles.about: Diplomatic telegram transmitting extensive Chinese and foreign press commentary on the assassination of Prime Minister Inukai Tsuyoshi and the rise of Japanese fascism.
subfiles.summary: U.S. Minister Nelson T. Johnson transmits an extensive compilation of Chinese vernacular and foreign press commentary analyzing the May 15, 1932 assassination of Japanese Prime Minister Inukai Tsuyoshi. Chinese editorials (including China Times, Shun Pao, Sin Wan Pao, Ta Kung Pao, and Central Daily News) view the murder as a militarist-fascist coup intended to dismantle party government and install an aggressive dictatorship. The papers delineate the key aims of Japanese fascism—including the annexation of Manchuria and Mongolia, direct rule under the Emperor, disregard of the League of Nations, conflict with the USSR and the United States, and the destruction of capitalism and parliamentary parties—and warn of intensified Japanese military pressure against China.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 548 from Nelson T. Johnson on Chinese Press Reactions to the Assassination of Prime Minister Inukai
